modules.title: 01. Markets, instruments and order books
modules.description: How exchanges work: instruments, order types, the limit order book, market makers, and how prices become returns.

lessons.title: Instruments, order types and the limit order book
objectives: Describe equities, futures and options and what each contract means.
Explain limit, market, IOC and stop orders and price-time priority matching.
Read an order book: bid, ask, spread, depth and market impact.

topics.title: Instruments
details: A share is ownership; a future is an agreement to trade later at a set price; a call option is the right (not obligation) to buy at a strike before expiry.
In India, NSE lists equities and very active index options (NIFTY, BANKNIFTY).

topics.title: Orders and matching
details: A limit order rests at a price; a market order takes the best available prices. The exchange matches by price, then time (first in, first out).

topics.title: Order book
details: Best bid and best ask define the spread; depth shows quantity at each level. Large orders walk the book and move the price (impact).
Market makers quote both sides and earn the spread while managing inventory risk.

reading.locator: OpenStax Principles of Finance: chapter 'Stocks and Stock Valuation' (sections on how stock markets work) and chapter on 'Derivatives' introduction.

assignment.title: Simulate a tiny order book
instructions: Write a Python order book supporting limit, market and cancel with price-time priority.
Feed it 20 hand-made orders; write the expected trades by hand first, then compare.
Compute spread and depth after each order.
deliverables: Code, hand-computed expected trades and comparison.
acceptanceCriteria: Trades match your hand-computed expectations exactly.

questions.prompt: What is the bid-ask spread?
questions.answer: The gap between the best ask and the best bid.

questions.prompt: How are two orders at the same price prioritised?
questions.answer: By time: the earlier order fills first.

reviewPrompts: Explain a call option in one sentence.
Why do large market orders move prices?

lessons.title: Prices, returns, compounding and corporate actions
objectives: Compute simple and log returns and annualise them correctly.
Adjust prices for splits and dividends before computing returns.
Load and clean daily price data for many stocks.

topics.title: Returns
details: Simple return r = P1/P0 - 1; log return = ln(P1/P0). Log returns add over time; simple returns aggregate across assets.
Annualise daily volatility by multiplying by sqrt(252).

topics.title: Adjustments
details: A 2-for-1 split halves the price without a loss; use adjusted prices or you will see fake crashes.

topics.title: Data hygiene
details: Check missing days, stale prices, outliers and survivorship (delisted stocks disappear from today's lists).

reading.locator: Zivot's Introduction to Computational Finance: chapter 1 'Return Calculations' (simple, continuously compounded, multi-period and portfolio returns).

assignment.title: Return toolkit
instructions: Download daily data for 10 NSE stocks from a public source and adjust for splits/dividends.
Compute daily simple and log returns, annualised mean and volatility, and a correlation matrix.
Show one example where unadjusted prices give a wrong return.
acceptanceCriteria: Annualisation uses sqrt(252) for volatility.
The split example is explained.

questions.prompt: Which returns add up over time?
questions.answer: Log returns.

questions.prompt: How do you annualise daily volatility?
questions.answer: Multiply by the square root of 252 trading days.

reviewPrompts: Simple vs log return?
What is survivorship bias?

modules.title: 02. Probability and statistics for quants
modules.description: The statistics behind every quant decision: distributions, estimation, hypothesis tests, regression and their traps in financial data.

lessons.title: Distributions, expectation, variance and fat tails
objectives: Fit normal and Student-t distributions to returns and compare tails.
Compute covariance and correlation and explain diversification.
Explain why expectation and variance are not enough for risk.

topics.title: Distributions
details: Daily returns have fat tails: extreme moves happen far more often than a normal model predicts. Check with QQ-plots and kurtosis.

topics.title: Covariance
details: Portfolio variance = w'Σw; low or negative correlation reduces risk. Correlations rise in crises, when diversification is needed most.

topics.title: Beyond variance
details: Skew and tail risk matter: two strategies with the same volatility can have very different worst days.

video.locator: Lectures on continuous random variables and the normal distribution.

reading.locator: Think Stats 3e: chapters on distributions, modelling distributions (including normal and lognormal) and relationships between variables (covariance and correlation).

assignment.title: Tails in real data
instructions: Fit normal and t distributions to NIFTY daily returns; plot QQ-plots.
Count days beyond 4 standard deviations versus what the normal model predicts.
Compute a two-asset portfolio's volatility for several correlations.
acceptanceCriteria: The tail comparison is quantified.
Portfolio volatility formula is verified by simulation.

questions.prompt: What does 'fat tails' mean?
questions.answer: Extreme outcomes occur more often than a normal distribution predicts.
questions.explanation: Visible in QQ-plots and high kurtosis.

questions.prompt: How does correlation affect portfolio risk?
questions.answer: Lower correlation reduces portfolio volatility.

reviewPrompts: Write the two-asset portfolio variance formula.
Why do correlations matter in crises?

lessons.title: Estimation, hypothesis tests, regression and multiple testing
objectives: Estimate a mean with a confidence interval and bootstrap it.
Run t-tests and regressions and interpret p-values correctly.
Explain multiple testing and how it creates fake strategies.

topics.title: Estimation
details: Sample means of returns are very noisy; a 1-year Sharpe estimate has a wide confidence interval.

topics.title: Tests and regression
details: A p-value is the chance of data this extreme if there were no effect, not the chance the effect is real. OLS regression estimates beta to the market.

topics.title: Multiple testing
details: Test 100 random strategies and about 5 look 'significant' at 5%. Adjust (Bonferroni, false discovery rate) and keep a holdout.

reading.locator: Think Stats 3e: chapters on estimation, hypothesis testing and linear least squares/regression.

assignment.title: Fool yourself on purpose
instructions: Generate 200 random 'strategies' (random signals) on real price data; find the best Sharpe.
Show how its out-of-sample performance collapses.
Apply a Bonferroni or FDR correction and explain the result.
Regress a stock's returns on NIFTY returns and interpret beta and R-squared.
acceptanceCriteria: The multiple-testing trap is demonstrated with numbers.

questions.prompt: What is a p-value?
questions.answer: The probability of results at least this extreme if the null hypothesis is true.
questions.explanation: It is not the probability the effect is real.

questions.prompt: Why do random strategies look good in backtests?
questions.answer: Testing many of them makes some succeed by chance.

reviewPrompts: Interpret beta = 1.2.
How do you protect against data snooping?

modules.title: 03. Modern C++ for performance
modules.description: C++ is the language of low-latency trading systems and pricing libraries. Learn modern C++ safely: ownership, the standard library, templates and tooling.

lessons.title: Values, references, RAII and smart pointers
objectives: Compile and run C++20 programs with warnings and sanitizers on.
Explain values, references, pointers and object lifetime.
Manage resources with RAII, unique_ptr and shared_ptr instead of new/delete.

topics.title: Basics
details: `g++ -std=c++20 -Wall -Wextra -O2 -fsanitize=address,undefined main.cpp` catches many bugs early.
References are aliases; pointers can be null; prefer references and values.

topics.title: Lifetime and RAII
details: An object's destructor runs when it goes out of scope; RAII ties resources (memory, files, locks) to object lifetime so they are always released.

topics.title: Smart pointers
details: unique_ptr: single owner, zero overhead; shared_ptr: shared ownership with a reference count. Raw `new`/`delete` in application code is a code smell.

reading.locator: LearnCpp.com: chapters 0-2 (setup and basics), 12 (references and pointers), 15 (classes and destructors) and 22 (move semantics and smart pointers).

assignment.title: Resource-safe order store
instructions: Write a C++20 OrderStore class that owns orders through unique_ptr and looks them up by ID.
Write a RAII ScopedTimer that prints elapsed time when destroyed.
Compile with sanitizers and fix every finding; write a short note on each bug.
deliverables: Code, build commands and sanitizer notes.
acceptanceCriteria: Builds with zero warnings and sanitizer findings.
No raw new/delete.

questions.prompt: What is RAII?
questions.answer: Tying a resource's lifetime to an object so its destructor releases it.
questions.explanation: Prevents leaks even when exceptions occur.

questions.prompt: When use unique_ptr vs shared_ptr?
questions.answer: unique_ptr for a single owner; shared_ptr only when ownership is truly shared.

reviewPrompts: Reference vs pointer?
Which compiler flags do you always use?

lessons.title: Standard library containers, algorithms and complexity
objectives: Choose vector, array, unordered_map, map and deque by access pattern.
Use standard algorithms and ranges instead of hand-written loops.
Measure the effect of memory layout on speed.

topics.title: Containers
details: vector is the default (contiguous, cache-friendly); unordered_map for O(1) average lookup; map for ordered keys (O(log n)); reserve() to avoid reallocations.

topics.title: Algorithms
details: std::sort, std::lower_bound, std::accumulate, std::ranges::find_if: clearer and often faster than loops.

topics.title: Layout
details: Linked structures scatter memory and cause cache misses; contiguous arrays are usually faster even with worse big-O for small n.

reading.locator: cppreference: 'Containers library' overview page (complexity table) and 'Algorithms library' overview; then std::vector and std::unordered_map pages.

assignment.title: Container shoot-out
instructions: Benchmark lookups and iteration for vector (sorted + binary search), map and unordered_map at sizes 100, 10,000 and 1,000,000.
Benchmark summing a vector versus a std::list of the same numbers.
Explain the results with cache behaviour.
deliverables: Benchmark code, results table and explanation.
acceptanceCriteria: Benchmarks use -O2 and repeat runs; results are explained.

questions.prompt: Default C++ container?
questions.answer: std::vector.

questions.prompt: Why can a list be slower than a vector for iteration?
questions.answer: List nodes are scattered in memory, causing cache misses.
questions.explanation: Big-O is the same, constants differ.

reviewPrompts: When would you choose std::map?
What does reserve() do?

lessons.title: Move semantics, templates, CMake and unit testing
objectives: Explain copy versus move and write move-friendly classes.
Write simple function and class templates.
Build a multi-file project with CMake and GoogleTest, and run it in CI.

topics.title: Moves
details: Moving transfers resources instead of copying (e.g. a vector's buffer); `std::move` casts to allow it. Follow the rule of zero where possible.

topics.title: Templates
details: Templates generate code per type at compile time: `template <typename T> T clamp(T v, T lo, T hi)`. C++20 concepts constrain them with readable errors.

topics.title: Build and test
details: CMake describes targets and dependencies; FetchContent pulls GoogleTest; `ctest` runs tests; GitHub Actions builds on every push.

reading.locator: CMake Tutorial steps 1-5 (basic project, libraries, usage requirements, generator expressions, installing and testing).

assignment.title: Pricing library skeleton
instructions: Create a CMake project with a library `pricing`, an executable and a GoogleTest suite.
Add a templated statistics helper (mean/variance) with tests for double and float.
Add a GitHub Actions workflow building with sanitizers and running ctest.
acceptanceCriteria: CI builds and tests on every push.

questions.prompt: What does std::move actually do?
questions.answer: Casts an object to an rvalue so a move constructor/assignment can be chosen.
questions.explanation: It does not move anything by itself.

questions.prompt: What is the rule of zero?
questions.answer: Let members manage resources so the class needs no custom copy/move/destructor.

reviewPrompts: Copy vs move?
Why use concepts with templates?

modules.title: 04. Time series analysis
modules.description: Model data that arrives over time: stationarity, autocorrelation, ARMA basics, and cointegration for pairs trading.

lessons.title: Stationarity, autocorrelation and ARMA basics
objectives: Test for stationarity (ADF) and transform series to make them stationary.
Read ACF/PACF plots.
Fit a simple ARMA model and evaluate forecasts out of sample.

topics.title: Stationarity
details: Prices wander (non-stationary); returns are closer to stationary. Many models assume stationarity, so difference or use returns.

topics.title: Autocorrelation
details: ACF shows correlation with past values; significant spikes suggest predictability (rare in liquid asset returns, common in volatility).

topics.title: Forecasting
details: Fit on the past, forecast forward, compare with a naive baseline (yesterday's value); always evaluate out of sample with time-ordered splits.

reading.locator: Forecasting: Principles and Practice: chapter 9 'ARIMA models' sections 9.1 (stationarity and differencing) through 9.5, and chapter 5.8 'Evaluating point forecast accuracy'.

assignment.title: Forecast honestly
instructions: Run ADF tests on NIFTY prices and returns; plot ACF/PACF of returns and squared returns.
Fit an ARMA model on returns with a time-based split and compare to a naive forecast.
Write what the squared-return ACF tells you about volatility.
acceptanceCriteria: Forecasts are evaluated only on later data than training.

questions.prompt: Are stock prices usually stationary?
questions.answer: No; returns are much closer to stationary.

questions.prompt: What baseline should a forecast beat?
questions.answer: A naive forecast such as the last observed value.

reviewPrompts: Explain the ADF test result.
What does volatility clustering look like in an ACF?

lessons.title: Cointegration and pairs trading
objectives: Explain cointegration versus correlation.
Test pairs with Engle-Granger and estimate the hedge ratio.
Build z-score entry/exit rules and check the half-life of mean reversion.

topics.title: Concept
details: Two prices can each wander but move together so their spread is stationary: that is cointegration. Correlated returns are not enough.

topics.title: Testing
details: Regress one price on the other to get the hedge ratio; test the residual spread for stationarity; beware multiple testing across many pairs.

topics.title: Trading rules
details: Enter when the spread's z-score exceeds about 2, exit near 0; estimate half-life to set holding periods; include costs.

reading.locator: statsmodels time series docs: the 'coint' and 'adfuller' function pages and the overview of stattools.

assignment.title: Find and test a pair
instructions: Test 20 candidate pairs of related NSE stocks (same sector) on a training period; correct for multiple testing.
For the best pair, compute hedge ratio, spread z-score and half-life.
Check whether cointegration holds in the following period.
deliverables: Notebook with tests, plots and out-of-period check.
acceptanceCriteria: The out-of-period result is reported honestly.

questions.prompt: Correlation vs cointegration?
questions.answer: Correlation is about co-movement of returns; cointegration means a combination of prices is stationary.

questions.prompt: What does the half-life of a spread tell you?
questions.answer: How quickly it tends to revert halfway to its mean.

reviewPrompts: Why test pairs only within sectors?
How can cointegration break?

modules.title: 05. Backtesting methodology
modules.description: Test strategies the way professional researchers do: event-driven simulation, realistic costs, and protection against bias and overfitting.

lessons.title: Event-driven backtesters, transaction costs and slippage
objectives: Design an event-driven backtester (data -> signal -> order -> fill -> portfolio).
Model brokerage, taxes, exchange fees and slippage for Indian markets.
Reconcile cash, positions and trades every day.

topics.title: Design
details: Process events in time order so a strategy can only see past data; vectorised backtests are fast but make look-ahead mistakes easy.

topics.title: Costs
details: Include brokerage, STT, exchange charges, GST, stamp duty and slippage; many strategies disappear after costs.

topics.title: Accounting
details: Cash + market value of positions must equal portfolio value; reconcile against the trade log daily.

reading.locator: QuantConnect 'Reality Modeling' key concepts: fees, slippage, fills and their effects on backtests.

assignment.title: Minimal event-driven backtester
instructions: Implement data feed, strategy, broker (fills with slippage), portfolio and cost model classes in Python.
Run a moving-average crossover on daily data for 5 NSE stocks.
Show results with and without costs and a daily reconciliation check.
acceptanceCriteria: Reconciliation passes every day.
Results are shown before and after costs.

questions.prompt: Why are event-driven backtests safer than vectorised ones?
questions.answer: They process data in time order, preventing look-ahead.
questions.explanation: Vectorised code can accidentally use future data.

questions.prompt: Name three costs to model in Indian equity trading.
questions.answer: Brokerage, STT and exchange transaction charges (also GST, stamp duty, slippage).

reviewPrompts: Draw the backtester event flow.
How do you model slippage simply?

lessons.title: Bias, overfitting and walk-forward validation
objectives: Identify look-ahead, survivorship and selection bias.
Use walk-forward validation and a final untouched holdout.
Report deflated, honest performance metrics.

topics.title: Biases
details: Look-ahead (using information before it was available), survivorship (only today's listed stocks), selection (reporting the best of many tries).

topics.title: Walk-forward
details: Optimise parameters on a window, trade the next window, roll forward; keep a final period you never touch until the end.

topics.title: Reporting
details: Report number of variants tried, out-of-sample results, costs and drawdowns, not just the best Sharpe.

reading.locator: QuantConnect Research Guide: sections on overfitting, look-ahead bias, survivorship bias and out-of-sample testing.

assignment.title: Bias audit
instructions: Add a walk-forward loop to your backtester.
Write tests that fail if future data is used (shift data and confirm past signals do not change).
Rerun the strategy with a point-in-time universe and report the difference survivorship made.
deliverables: Code, tests and a bias audit report.
acceptanceCriteria: The look-ahead test exists and passes.
Out-of-sample results are reported even if worse.

questions.prompt: What is survivorship bias?
questions.answer: Testing only on assets that still exist today, ignoring delisted ones.

questions.prompt: Why keep an untouched holdout?
questions.answer: To get one unbiased estimate after all tuning is done.
questions.explanation: Every look at it leaks information.

reviewPrompts: Describe walk-forward validation.
What do you report besides Sharpe?

modules.title: 06. Derivatives pricing
modules.description: Price options with Black-Scholes, binomial trees and Monte Carlo, compute Greeks, and build implied volatility surfaces.

lessons.title: Black-Scholes, Greeks and put-call parity
objectives: State the Black-Scholes assumptions and price European options.
Compute and interpret delta, gamma, vega, theta and rho.
Check prices with put-call parity.

topics.title: Model
details: Assumes lognormal prices with constant volatility and rate, no arbitrage and continuous hedging; gives closed-form prices for European options.

topics.title: Greeks
details: Delta: price sensitivity to the underlying (hedge ratio). Gamma: how delta changes. Vega: sensitivity to volatility. Theta: time decay.

topics.title: Parity
details: C - P = S - K e^(-rT) for European options without dividends; violations signal data errors or arbitrage.

reading.locator: OpenStax Principles of Finance: derivatives chapter sections on options and option pricing.

assignment.title: Black-Scholes in C++ and Python
instructions: Implement Black-Scholes prices and Greeks in C++ and expose to Python (pybind11) or write in both languages.
Verify against QuantLib on a grid of strikes and expiries.
Check put-call parity on cleaned NIFTY option quotes.
deliverables: Code, tests against QuantLib and parity check.
acceptanceCriteria: Prices match QuantLib within a small tolerance.
Greeks are checked by finite differences.

questions.prompt: What does delta measure?
questions.answer: How much the option price changes for a small change in the underlying.
questions.explanation: It is also the hedge ratio.

questions.prompt: State put-call parity.
questions.answer: C - P = S - K e^(-rT).

reviewPrompts: List the Black-Scholes assumptions.
Why is theta usually negative for long options?

lessons.title: Binomial trees and Monte Carlo with variance reduction
objectives: Price European and American options with a CRR binomial tree.
Price options by Monte Carlo and report standard errors.
Reduce Monte Carlo error with antithetic and control variates.

topics.title: Trees
details: Step the price up or down with risk-neutral probabilities; work backwards from expiry; check early exercise at each node for American options.

topics.title: Monte Carlo
details: Simulate many price paths, average discounted payoffs; error shrinks with 1/sqrt(N), so 4x paths halve the error.

topics.title: Variance reduction
details: Antithetic variates pair each path with its mirror; control variates use a related option with a known price to cancel noise.

video.locator: Lectures on stochastic processes and Black-Scholes (Ito calculus lectures).

reading.locator: Zivot: the chapters on estimator properties and the bootstrap, where Monte Carlo simulation and standard errors of simulated estimates are introduced.

assignment.title: Three pricers, one answer
instructions: Price the same European call with Black-Scholes, a binomial tree (show convergence as steps grow) and Monte Carlo.
Add antithetic and control variates; compare standard errors at equal path counts.
Price an American put with the tree and explain the early-exercise premium.
deliverables: Code, convergence plots and error table.
acceptanceCriteria: All three methods agree within reported error.
Variance reduction is measured.

questions.prompt: How does Monte Carlo error scale with paths?
questions.answer: With 1 over the square root of the number of paths.

questions.prompt: Why can American options be worth more than European?
questions.answer: They can be exercised early.
questions.explanation: Valuable for puts when deep in the money.

reviewPrompts: Explain backward induction.
How do control variates work?

lessons.title: Implied volatility, the volatility smile and SVI surfaces
objectives: Solve for implied volatility with a robust root finder (see the rootfinding chapter of Fundamentals of Numerical Computation).
Explain the volatility smile/skew and term structure.
Fit an SVI curve per expiry and check for arbitrage.

topics.title: Implied vol
details: The volatility that makes Black-Scholes match the market price; solve with Brent's method within bounds; skip quotes with no bid.

topics.title: Smile and skew
details: Index options usually show higher implied vol for low strikes (skew): the market prices crash risk.

topics.title: SVI
details: SVI parameterises total implied variance per expiry with five parameters; check butterfly (no negative densities) and calendar (variance grows with time) conditions.

reading.locator: Gatheral and Jacquier: sections 2-3 (SVI parameterisation and no-arbitrage conditions).

assignment.title: Build a NIFTY vol surface
instructions: Clean end-of-day NIFTY option quotes for three expiries; compute implied vols.
Fit SVI per expiry; plot the smile and the 3D surface.
Run butterfly and calendar arbitrage checks and report any violations.
acceptanceCriteria: The fitted surface passes checks or violations are explained.

questions.prompt: What is implied volatility?
questions.answer: The volatility input that makes the model price equal the market price.
questions.explanation: The market's view of future volatility.

questions.prompt: What does index skew reflect?
questions.answer: Higher demand for downside protection (crash risk).

reviewPrompts: Explain calendar arbitrage.
Why use Brent's method for implied vol?

modules.title: 07. Low-latency engineering
modules.description: Why some code is 100x faster than equivalent code: CPU caches, memory allocation, lock-free queues, and measuring it properly.

lessons.title: CPU caches, memory layout and allocation
objectives: Explain cache lines, the cache hierarchy and false sharing.
Design data layouts (structure of arrays, preallocated pools) for speed.
Profile with perf to find cache misses and hotspots.

topics.title: Caches
details: L1 ~1 ns, L2 ~4 ns, L3 ~10-20 ns, main memory ~100 ns. Data moves in 64-byte cache lines; sequential access is fastest.

topics.title: Layout and allocation
details: Avoid pointer chasing; keep hot fields together; preallocate object pools so the hot path never calls malloc.

topics.title: Measuring
details: `perf stat -e cache-misses,instructions` and `perf record`/`perf report`; benchmark with warm-up and many repetitions.

video.locator: MIT 6.172 lecture on caches/cache-efficient algorithms (as linked).

reading.locator: What Every Programmer Should Know About Memory: section 3 'CPU Caches' (3.1-3.3) and section 6 'What Programmers Can Do' (6.1-6.2).

assignment.title: Measure the memory wall
instructions: Benchmark summing an array with sequential versus random access at sizes from 16 KB to 1 GB; plot ns per element.
Create false sharing between two threads and fix it with alignas(64).
Profile one of your programs with perf and fix a hotspot.
deliverables: Benchmarks, plots, perf output and fixes.
acceptanceCriteria: Cache-size boundaries are visible in the plot.
False sharing fix is measured.

questions.prompt: How big is a typical cache line?
questions.answer: 64 bytes.
questions.explanation: Data moves between memory and cache in lines.

questions.prompt: What is false sharing?
questions.answer: Threads writing different variables on the same cache line, forcing it to bounce between cores.

reviewPrompts: List latency numbers for L1, L3 and RAM.
Why avoid malloc in the hot path?

lessons.title: Atomics, memory ordering and lock-free SPSC queues
objectives: Explain atomics and acquire/release ordering.
Implement a bounded single-producer single-consumer ring buffer.
Test concurrent code with ThreadSanitizer and measure latency percentiles.

topics.title: Atomics
details: std::atomic operations are indivisible; memory_order_release on a write and acquire on the matching read guarantee the data written before is visible.

topics.title: SPSC queue
details: With one producer and one consumer, a ring buffer with atomic head and tail indices needs no locks; pad indices to separate cache lines.

topics.title: Testing
details: Run under -fsanitize=thread; stress test with billions of items; report p50/p99/p99.9 latency, not just averages.

reading.locator: cppreference std::memory_order: read the explanation of relaxed, release-acquire and sequentially consistent ordering with the examples.

assignment.title: SPSC ring buffer
instructions: Implement a bounded SPSC queue with acquire/release atomics and cache-line padding.
Compare throughput and latency percentiles with a mutex-protected std::queue.
Run 1 billion transfers under TSan (smaller count is fine) and verify order and completeness.
acceptanceCriteria: No TSan reports; every item arrives once and in order.

questions.prompt: What does release-acquire ordering guarantee?
questions.answer: Writes before the release are visible to the thread that acquires the same atomic.

questions.prompt: Why report p99 latency, not just the mean?
questions.answer: Rare slow events matter in trading and are hidden by averages.

reviewPrompts: Explain why SPSC can be lock-free simply.
What does TSan detect?

modules.title: 08. Risk and portfolio construction
modules.description: Measure risk the way risk managers do and build portfolios: Sharpe, drawdown, VaR, expected shortfall and mean-variance optimisation.

lessons.title: Risk metrics: Sharpe, drawdown, VaR and expected shortfall
objectives: Compute Sharpe, Sortino, maximum drawdown and Calmar from returns.
Estimate VaR and expected shortfall historically and parametrically.
Backtest VaR by counting breaches.

topics.title: Performance
details: Sharpe = (mean excess return / volatility) x sqrt(252) for daily data; drawdown is the fall from a previous peak.

topics.title: Tail risk
details: 95% 1-day VaR: a loss exceeded on about 5% of days. Expected shortfall: the average loss on those worst days (more informative).

topics.title: Validation
details: Count VaR breaches over time; far more than expected means the model underestimates risk.

reading.locator: Zivot: chapters on descriptive statistics for returns and risk measures (value-at-risk) in the computational finance text.

assignment.title: Risk report
instructions: For your backtested strategy and NIFTY, compute Sharpe, Sortino, max drawdown, VaR and ES.
Backtest historical VaR by counting breaches.
Write a one-page risk report a portfolio manager could read.
acceptanceCriteria: Metrics are computed from daily data with correct annualisation.

questions.prompt: What is maximum drawdown?
questions.answer: The largest peak-to-trough fall in portfolio value.

questions.prompt: Why prefer expected shortfall over VaR?
questions.answer: It measures how bad losses are beyond the VaR threshold.

reviewPrompts: Compute annualised Sharpe from daily numbers.
How do you test a VaR model?

lessons.title: Portfolio construction and mean-variance optimisation
objectives: Compute the efficient frontier for a set of assets.
Explain why naive optimisation is unstable and how to regularise it.
Compare equal-weight, minimum-variance and risk-parity portfolios out of sample.

topics.title: Markowitz
details: Minimise variance for a target return; the result is very sensitive to estimated expected returns.

topics.title: Stability
details: Use shrinkage covariance, constraints (no shorting, weight caps) or simpler rules; equal weight is a strong baseline.

topics.title: Comparison
details: Rebalance monthly in a walk-forward test and compare risk-adjusted returns after costs.

reading.locator: Zivot: chapters on portfolio theory (Markowitz) and the efficient frontier.

assignment.title: Three portfolios
instructions: Using 10-20 NSE stocks, build equal-weight, minimum-variance (with shrinkage) and risk-parity portfolios.
Walk-forward with monthly rebalancing and costs; compare metrics.
acceptanceCriteria: Comparison is out of sample and includes costs.

questions.prompt: Why is mean-variance optimisation unstable?
questions.answer: It is very sensitive to noisy expected-return estimates.
questions.explanation: Small input changes cause big weight changes.

questions.prompt: Why is equal weight a good baseline?
questions.answer: It needs no estimates and is hard to beat out of sample.

reviewPrompts: What is the efficient frontier?
Explain risk parity.

modules.title: 09. Quant interview preparation
modules.description: Quant developer and researcher interviews mix probability puzzles, mental maths, market-making games, coding and C++ questions.

lessons.title: Probability puzzles, expected value, mental maths and market making
objectives: Solve classic probability and expected-value puzzles quickly and explain them.
Do fast mental arithmetic and estimation.
Play a market-making game: quote a spread, update on information, manage inventory.

topics.title: Puzzles
details: Conditioning, symmetry, linearity of expectation and recursion solve most puzzles (e.g. expected flips to get HH = 6).

topics.title: Mental maths
details: Practise multiplication, fractions and percentages under time pressure; estimate before computing.

topics.title: Market making
details: Quote a bid and ask around your fair value; widen when uncertain; shift quotes as you accumulate inventory or learn information.

reading.locator: probabilitycourse.com: review conditional probability, expectation and linearity of expectation examples; then attempt the end-of-chapter problems.

assignment.title: Interview drill
instructions: Solve 30 puzzles on Brainstellar (10 easy, 15 medium, 5 hard); log time and approach.
Do 10 minutes of mental maths drills on 10 days and record scores.
Play a market-making game with a friend (e.g. guessing the sum of cards) and write what you learned.
deliverables: Puzzle log, drill scores and game notes.
acceptanceCriteria: Each puzzle has a written explanation, not just the answer.

questions.prompt: Expected number of fair coin flips to get two heads in a row?
What should a market maker do when unsure of fair value?
questions.answer: Quote a wider spread.

reviewPrompts: Explain linearity of expectation with an example.
How do you adjust quotes when long inventory?

sources.title: MIT 18.S096 Topics in Mathematics with Applications in Finance

limitations: Skill-builder lessons are beginner-first: each one assumes you have not used the tool before and explains the vocabulary before the practice.
Readings are official documentation or free books, linked rather than copied. Check the current version when you open a link; tools change.
Use your own machine, free tiers and synthetic or public data. Never use employer code, client data or credentials in exercises.
Paper-only: no live broker connections or real orders. Backtest results are research evidence, not investment advice or proof of profitable trading.

stageOutcomes.outcome: Write modern, tested C++ and analyse time series and backtests honestly.
stageOutcomes.evidence: A CMake C++ project with tests, plus a backtest with costs and walk-forward validation.

stageOutcomes.outcome: Price options with several methods, build volatility surfaces and engineer low-latency code.
stageOutcomes.evidence: Pricers cross-checked with QuantLib and benchmarked lock-free components.

stageOutcomes.outcome: Measure risk and construct portfolios, and pass quant interviews.
